newsitem.title: CHINA: Does Thai crisis look like Mexico? Not yet.
newsitem.headline: Does Thai crisis look like Mexico? Not yet.

text.p: Comparisons between Thailand in 1997 and Mexico in late 1994 are unfair, partly because there is little fear at this point that the Thai government is insolvent, economists said on Thursday.

"So far, the crisis we've seen in Thailand has been a currency crisis," said Nicholas Kwan, chief economist at Merrill Lynch. "But in Mexico's case we had not just a currency crisis but a government default crisis."

Thailand's sovereign debt amounts to about US$17 billion, and sovereign spreads barely moved when speculators concerned about the nation's high foreign liabilities, wide current account deficit and cash-strapped banking sector forced a de facto devaluation of the Thai baht on July 2.

"This is a private sector problem," said economist Irene Cheung at Merrill Lynch. "The government has not been borrowing much, it's been keeping debt at a comfortable level and these borrowings are mostly between governments. This is not over-gearing in the government."
Merrill Lynch did not want to understate the severity of the problems confronted by Thailand following a more than 20-percent depreciation in the baht.

"Any depreciation over 15-20 percent (poses) serious problems to company cash flow and loan repayment ability," Cheung said. "Significant loan defaults, business failure and layoffs could push the economy close to a recession in the near term."
Most of Thailand's problems stem from a large proportion of foreign-denominated debt issued by domestic banks and finance companies loaded with bad loans, she said.

The biggest damage of the Mexican crisis was done not by the peso's devaluation in late December 1994 but by the Mexican government's failure to roll over its Tesobono debt (Mexican government treasuries) in the early weeks of 1995.
"When the government was confirmed insolvent, the currency crisis quickly degenerated into a full-blown economic disaster," Kwan said.

Akin with most other East Asian economies, Thailand has kept relatively strong fiscal discipline, reporting fiscal surpluses in nine of the past 10 years and maintaining a fiscal reserve of about BT400 billion, he said.

"While part of the pressure on the Thai baht came from the government's initial large budget deficit, Bangkok's relatively prompt decision to slash budget spending and the government's sizeable fiscal reserve helped to prevent the currency crisis from developing into a bigger confidence crisis on government solvency," he said.

Kwan said Thailand also will benefit from a benign U.S. interest rate environment, at least for the time being. U.S. Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan suggested this week that rates would remain unchanged in the short-term.
By comparison, Mexico fell victim to a major reversal in capital flows triggered by repeated increases in U.S. interest rates starting in early 1994.

Ken Davies, senior regional economist at the Economist Intelligence Unit, said Mexico did not have Thailand's high savings rate. Mexico's current account deficit also consisted less of investment into productive capital goods -- a key confidence factor among emerging economies.
Investors tend to worry less about current account deficits if they know the borrowing was spent on capital goods to enhance future output rather than on consumer items.
"Thailand's (proportion of the current account devoted to consumer goods) wasn't that low, one mustn't exaggerate this, but it's worth bearing in mind," Davies said.
Asia's heavier dependence upon foreign direct investment than on volatile portfolio flows also works in its favour, Merrill Lynch said.
In 1996, FDI accounted for 53 percent of net capital flows to Asia compared to Latin America's 24 percent in 1996 and 26 percent in 1994.
